Understanding the approach

The connection between methods matters.

BACP describes integrative counselling as drawing on more than one therapeutic approach and adapting the work to the person. It may bring together attention to thoughts, emotions, behavior, relationships, and experience. The aim is not to use as many techniques as possible; it is to make choices that fit the person and the purpose of care.

Integration can take different forms. A clinician may have a main theoretical orientation while using selected elements from another approach, or may work from an established integrative framework. A biography that names several methods does not by itself explain how they are combined or establish a separate integrative certification.

A coherent plan should connect the assessment, goals, proposed methods, and review of progress. Flexibility is useful when it responds to what is happening, not when it means unexplained changes of direction. The clinician should remain within their training and scope when selecting any technique.

Sources integrative psychotherapy

In plain language

One question can organize the work.

How does this part of therapy relate to the change I am hoping for? A plain-language answer should connect the activity to the plan rather than ask you to trust a label.

A worked example

A boundary problem needs more than one kind of attention.

A fictional example of combining perspectives around one agreed goal.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

The practical difficulty

Avery repeatedly accepts extra responsibilities, becomes exhausted, and then withdraws from people they care about.

02

Different parts of the pattern

A clinician might help Avery notice a belief about disappointing others, understand the feelings around saying no, and rehearse a clearer response.

03

The shared purpose

These elements connect to one goal: making commitments more deliberately and protecting time for what matters. They are not separate activities added only for variety.

How would the clinician know whether the combination is useful?

The work could be reviewed against changes Avery recognizes outside therapy: understanding the pressure, making a different choice, or recovering more effectively after an overcommitment. If practice feels impossible, the plan may need to examine safety, resources, relationship dynamics, or another obstacle.

The example does not prescribe which approaches Avery needs. It illustrates the importance of an understandable connection between the problem, the methods, and the review of progress.

Sources integrative psychotherapy

Go a little deeper

Four questions that make integration visible.

A client does not need technical training to ask for a coherent explanation.

01What is the main understanding?The plan should have more structure than a list of methods.Read more +

Ask how the clinician understands the difficulty so far and what remains uncertain. This helps explain why a particular activity is proposed.

An initial understanding can change as new information emerges, but the change should be discussed.

02What is this method intended to do?Connect the activity to the agreed goal.Read more +

A practical exercise may target a behavioral pattern; a reflective conversation may clarify meaning or a relationship experience. The clinician can explain the purpose without promising a result.

You can ask about alternatives when a method does not fit your preferences or circumstances.

03How does it fit your training?Flexibility does not remove scope boundaries.Read more +

A therapist should have relevant preparation for the methods they use. Combining approaches does not justify offering a specialized intervention without adequate competence.

Published-profile descriptions are starting information, not a complete verification of every credential.

04How will we review it?Adaptation should be informed by what happens.Read more +

Progress can include symptoms, functioning, relationships, or other agreed goals. A technique can be revised or stopped when it is not appropriate.

The plan should not become a series of unexplained experiments with no shared direction.

Sources integrative psychotherapy

Inside the work

Assessment, choice, feedback, and revision.

01

Understand the person and context

Clarify concerns, goals, strengths, preferences, safety, and practical circumstances.

02

Explain a starting plan

Connect the proposed methods to the current understanding and invite questions or disagreement.

03

Work collaboratively

Use the agreed elements while attending to the client's experience and what occurs outside appointments.

04

Review and adapt

Discuss what is useful, what is not, and whether the plan, approach, or service needs to change.

Sources integrative psychotherapy

Fit, choice and limitations

More approaches do not automatically produce better care.

Not a claim of universal effectiveness

A broad integrative label does not show that every combination has been studied or fits every condition. Evidence, training, and the individual's needs still matter.

Not the same as a certification list

A profile describing several approaches can show a varied style. It does not establish a distinct integrative credential or guarantee expertise in every technique within those approaches.

Sources integrative psychotherapy

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

Do I need to choose all the methods before starting?

No. You can begin with the concern and your preferences. The clinician should explain a proposed plan and help you understand unfamiliar terms.

Is integrative therapy the same as eclectic therapy?

The terms can overlap in everyday use, but they do not always mean the same thing to different clinicians. Ask how the therapist connects their methods and what framework guides the choices rather than relying on the label alone.

Can I prefer practical work over reflective conversation?

Yes. Your preferences matter, though the clinician may explain why another element could be relevant. A collaborative plan makes room for that discussion rather than assuming one style fits everyone.

What if the direction changes from week to week?

Ask how the changes connect to the goals and the clinician's understanding. Flexibility can be appropriate, but you should not be left unable to understand the purpose of the work.

Which M.F.T. clinicians use integrative therapy?

Several biographies describe more than one approach, but that alone does not establish an explicit integrative-therapy designation. This guide does not infer a method-specific credential or provider match from a long list of modalities.

How can I compare it with CBT or person-centered therapy?

The CBT guide explains one family of models, while person-centered therapy emphasizes a particular therapeutic relationship. An integrative clinician should explain what they draw from each and why.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
